Stock Market Reaction to Major News Events¶

A Data Analyst Portfolio Project
Python | Pandas | NumPy | EDA | Data Transformation | Statistical Analysis | Power BI

Business Question¶

When major news affects a company, how does its stock react, how long does the reaction last, and does the price recover afterwards?

What I wanted to understand¶

  • How strongly does a stock react on the first trading day after major news?
  • Does the reaction continue over the following 10 trading days?
  • Do some types of news create stronger or longer-lasting reactions?
  • Do large price drops or jumps tend to reverse?
  • Are the observed reactions different from what could happen on ordinary trading days?
  • Which companies and event categories show the strongest reactions?

Project Scope¶

  • Companies: 20 large companies
  • News period: 2025
  • Financial news source: FinDailyKG, built from GDELT
  • Market data: Yahoo Finance
  • Benchmark: SPY / S&P 500 ETF
  • Analysis window: Day -1 to Day +10
  • Output: Analysis tables and Power BI-ready CSV files

Skills Demonstrated¶

ETL-style Data Preparation → EDA → Data Cleaning → Data Transformation → Financial Analysis → Statistical Analysis → Data Visualization → Power BI

This project is an analytical ETL workflow rather than a dedicated data-engineering pipeline.
The focus is on preparing real-world data correctly before analysis.

Analytical Workflow¶

1. Extract¶

  • Read financial news data from Parquet files.
  • Extract organisation/article relationships for the selected companies.
  • Obtain historical stock prices for the companies and SPY.

2. Transform¶

  • Clean and standardise headlines.
  • Map company names to stock tickers.
  • Remove duplicate company-article relationships.
  • Identify relevant business events.
  • Categorise events using business-event keywords.
  • Remove irrelevant financial-news noise.
  • Convert publication timestamps to New York time.
  • Assign each headline to the trading day that could react to it.
  • Calculate daily returns and abnormal returns.
  • Create event-level reaction windows.

3. Load¶

  • Create cleaned analytical tables.
  • Export event-level, category-level and company-level results.
  • Create long-format data suitable for Power BI.

4. Explore¶

  • Examine event distributions.
  • Compare companies and event categories.
  • Analyse abnormal-return patterns.
  • Study persistence and recovery.

5. Analyse¶

  • Calculate abnormal returns and CAR.
  • Compare reactions with random trading days.
  • Run statistical tests.
  • Interpret the results carefully without claiming causality.

Data Understanding and Initial EDA¶

Before transforming the data, I first looked at how the source data was organised.

The FinDailyKG data contains three main tables:

Table Purpose
articles News article headline, time, website and URL
article_org_edges Links between articles and organisations
org_universe Organisation names appearing in the dataset

The organisation-to-article relationship table is large, so I later filter it to the 20 companies used in this study.

EDA objective at this stage¶

I want to understand:

  • how many organisations are present,
  • which organisations have the most articles,
  • how the source data is structured,
  • and what information is available before beginning the cleaning process.

This initial inspection helps avoid making assumptions about the raw dataset.

Company Selection and Data Mapping¶

The same company can appear under different names in a news dataset.

For example, a company may appear as:

  • company name
  • company corporation
  • company inc.
  • abbreviated company name

I therefore create a simple mapping between:

Dataset organisation name → Company → Stock ticker

This is an important data-transformation step because the news data and stock-price data use different identifiers.

Why this matters¶

Without consistent identifiers, the news events could not be matched reliably to the corresponding stock prices.

ETL: Build the News Analysis Table¶

This is the main data preparation stage of the project.

Extract¶

I extract only the article-company relationships relevant to my selected companies.

Transform¶

I then:

  • remove duplicate company-article relationships,
  • attach article headlines and timestamps,
  • map companies to stock tickers,
  • convert GDELT timestamps into usable datetime values,
  • remove incomplete records,
  • create a lowercase headline field for text-based filtering.

The goal is to create one clean table that can be used for the event analysis.

ETL note: This project uses ETL-style data extraction and transformation for analytical purposes. It is not presented as a production ETL pipeline.

In [7]:
# Extract only the columns and companies needed for the analysis
edges = pd.read_parquet(

    filters=[

    ],
)

    "tone_score",
    na_position="last"

edges = edges.drop_duplicates(

articles = pd.read_parquet(
    DATA_FOLDER / "articles_2025.parquet",
    columns=[
        "article_id",
        "seendate",
        "title",
        "domain",
        "url"
    ],
)

articles = articles.drop_duplicates("article_id")

news = edges.merge(
    articles,
    on="article_id",
    how="inner"
)

news["ticker"] = news["company"].map(
    company_to_ticker
)

# Convert GDELT timestamp to UTC datetime
news["published_utc"] = pd.to_datetime(
    news["seendate"],
    format="%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ",
    utc=True,
    errors="coerce"
)

news["headline"] = (
    news["title"]
    .fillna("")
    .str.strip()
)

news = news[
    (news["headline"] != "") &
    news["published_utc"].notna()
].copy()

news["headline_lc"] = news["headline"].str.lower()

log = [
    ("Company-article pairs", len(news))
]

print("Company-article pairs:", len(news))

display(
    news[
        ["company", "published_utc", "headline"]
    ].head()

EDA + Event Identification¶

At this point I have a news table, but not every news article should be treated as a market event.

Exploratory question¶

What type of information is actually present in the headlines?

For this project I focus on headlines describing a meaningful company or business event, such as:

  • earnings and guidance,
  • acquisitions and major deals,
  • leadership changes,
  • legal or regulatory developments,
  • products and business changes,
  • macroeconomic or geopolitical developments.

I remove headlines that are mainly:

  • analyst opinions,
  • fund/share holdings,
  • market commentary,
  • earnings previews,
  • general stock forecasts.

This step combines EDA, text-based data cleaning and business-rule transformation.

In [9]:
def has_any(text, words):
    # Whole-word matching prevents accidental matches
    pattern = (
        r"\b(?:"
        + "|".join(re.escape(w) for w in words)
        + r")\b"
    )

    return text.str.contains(
        pattern,
        regex=True
    )


# The company must appear in the headline
named = pd.Series(
    False,
    index=news.index
)

for company, words in headline_words.items():
    rows = news["company"] == company

    named.loc[rows] = has_any(
        news.loc[rows, "headline_lc"],
        words
    )

news = news[named].copy()

log.append(
    ("Company named in headline", len(news))
)


# Remove company-name lookalikes
for company, phrases in lookalikes.items():

    bad = (
        (news["company"] == company)
        &
        news["headline_lc"].str.contains(
            "|".join(phrases),
            regex=True
        )
    )

    news = news[~bad]

log.append(
    ("Look-alikes removed", len(news))
)

print(log[-3:])

[('Company-article pairs', 195023), ('Company named in headline', 16543), ('Look-alikes removed', 16529)]

share_count_rule = (
    r"\b(?:acquires|acquired|buys|bought|sells|sold|"
    r"purchases|purchased)\s+\d[\d,\. ]*\s*shares"
)


def is_noise(text):

    result = text.str.contains(
        share_count_rule,
        regex=True
    )

    for words in noise_words.values():
        result = result | has_any(
            text,
            words
        )

    return result


before = len(candidates)

candidates = candidates[
    ~is_noise(
        candidates["headline_lc"]
    )
].copy()

log.append(
    ("Noise removed", len(candidates))
)

print(
    "Removed",
    before - len(candidates),
    "noise headlines."
)

print(
    "Left:",
    len(candidates)
)

def noise(headline):
    return bool(
        is_noise(
            pd.Series([headline.lower()])
        ).iloc[0]
    )


assert noise(
    "Acme Capital Acquires 665 Shares of The Boeing Company"
)

assert noise(
    "Goldman Sachs raises Tesla price target to $400"
)

assert noise(
    "Stock Market Today: Dow Jones rises as Nvidia jumps"
)

assert not noise(
    "Netflix reports record quarterly earnings"
)

assert not noise(
    "Nvidia to buy Run:ai in $700 million deal, shares jump"
)

Stock Price Data¶

I now bring in the second major data source: historical stock prices.

I use adjusted closing prices so that stock splits and dividends are reflected in the price series.

The 20 companies are compared with SPY, which is used as a broad market benchmark.

EDA check¶

Before calculating reactions, I check:

  • number of trading days,
  • date range,
  • missing prices,
  • price-data availability.

This prevents incomplete market data from silently affecting the event analysis.

Assigning the Reaction Day¶

News timestamps need to be connected to actual trading days.

I convert the publication time to New York time and use the following rule:

News timing Day 0
Trading day before 4 PM Same trading day
Trading day at/after 4 PM Next trading day
Weekend or market holiday Next trading day

Day 0 therefore represents the first trading day on which the market could reasonably react to the headline.

This transformation is important because a calendar date and a stock-market trading date are not always the same.

In [16]:
trading_dates = set(
    prices.index.date
)


def find_reaction_day(
    published_utc,
    trading_dates
):

    ny_time = published_utc.tz_convert(
        "America/New_York"
    )

    day = ny_time.date()

    if ny_time.hour >= MARKET_CLOSE_HOUR:
        day = day + timedelta(days=1)

    while day not in trading_dates:
        day = day + timedelta(days=1)

    if day > max(trading_dates):
        return pd.NaT

    return day


# Small checks for the trading-day logic
test_days = {
    pd.Timestamp(d).date()
    for d in [
        "2025-01-02",
        "2025-01-03",
        "2025-01-06"
    ]
}


def check(utc_text, expected):

    result = find_reaction_day(
        pd.Timestamp(
            utc_text,
            tz="UTC"
        ),
        test_days
    )

    assert str(result) == expected


check(
    "2025-01-02 14:00",
    "2025-01-02"
)

check(
    "2025-01-03 20:59",
    "2025-01-03"
)

check(
    "2025-01-03 21:00",
    "2025-01-06"
)

check(
    "2025-01-04 15:00",
    "2025-01-06"
)

check(
    "2025-01-01 15:00",
    "2025-01-02"
)

Event Deduplication¶

The same real-world event can appear in many different news articles.

If every article were treated as a separate event, one stock movement could be counted multiple times.

Therefore, I keep one event for each:

Company + Reaction Day + Event Category

I retain the earliest article and record how many articles were associated with that event.

This is another important data-cleaning and transformation step before analysis.

Event-Based Financial Analysis¶

Now that the news data has been cleaned and the events have been identified, I measure the stock-market reaction.

For every event I collect abnormal returns from:

Day -1 → Day 0 → Day +1 → ... → Day +10

Key measures¶

Abnormal Return (AR)
Company return − SPY return

Day 0
The first trading day on which the market could react to the news.

Cumulative Abnormal Return (CAR)
The cumulative abnormal return over a period.

For example:

CAR 0-3 = AR Day 0 + AR Day 1 + AR Day 2 + AR Day 3

Day -1 is retained as a pre-event check to see whether some of the movement may have happened before the identified news reaction day.

In [20]:
rows = []

for _, event in events.iterrows():

    position = prices.index.get_loc(
        event["reaction_date"]
    )

    window = abnormal[
        event["ticker"]
    ].iloc[
        position - 1:
        position + 11
    ].tolist()

    window = (
        window +
        [np.nan] * (12 - len(window))
    )

    rows.append(window)


ar_columns = (
    ["AR_before"] +
    [
        f"AR_day{d}"
        for d in range(0, 11)
    ]
)

events = events.join(
    pd.DataFrame(
        rows,
        columns=ar_columns
    )
)


for k in [1, 3, 5, 10]:

    columns = [
        f"AR_day{d}"
        for d in range(0, k + 1)
    ]

    events[
        f"CAR_0_{k}"
    ] = events[
        columns
    ].sum(
        axis=1,
        skipna=False
    )


complete = events[
    ar_columns[1:]
].notna().all(axis=1)

print(
    "Events with a complete Day 0 to Day 10 window:",
    complete.sum(),
    "of",
    len(events)
)

Persistence Analysis¶

A strong Day 0 reaction does not necessarily mean the effect lasted.

I therefore compare the cumulative reaction through Day 10 with the original Day 0 reaction.

Persistence ratio¶

Persistence ratio = CAR 0-10 / AR Day 0

Interpretation:

  • 1.0 → the Day 0 move was broadly maintained
  • 0.5 → at least half of the initial move remained
  • below 0 → the reaction moved past the original starting point in the opposite direction

I classify a reaction as Persisted when at least 50% of the Day 0 move remains in the same direction by Day 10.

In [24]:
events["ratio_day10"] = (
    events["CAR_0_10"]
    /
    events["AR_day0"]
)

events["ratio_day10"] = (
    events["ratio_day10"]
    .replace(
        [np.inf, -np.inf],
        np.nan
    )
)

events["persisted"] = (
    events["ratio_day10"]
    >= PERSIST_RATIO
).astype(float)

events.loc[
    events["ratio_day10"].isna(),
    "persisted"
] = np.nan

events["persistence_status"] = np.where(
    events["ratio_day10"] >= PERSIST_RATIO,
    "Persisted",
    np.where(
        events["ratio_day10"] < 0,
        "Reversed",
        "Faded"
    )
)

events.loc[
    events["ratio_day10"].isna(),
    "persistence_status"
] = None

print(
    "Persisted in",
    round(
        events["persisted"].mean() * 100,
        1
    ),
    "% of events"
)

events[
    "persistence_status"
].value_counts()

Recovery and Give-Back Analysis¶

I next focus on larger initial reactions.

A move of 1% or more in abnormal return on Day 0 is treated as a large first move.

For these events I calculate how much of the original move had reversed by Day 5 and Day 10.

Interpretation¶

For a large drop:

% reversed = recovery

For a large jump:

% reversed = give-back

A value of 100% means the original move had fully reversed.

A negative value means the move became larger rather than reversing.

In [25]:
# Recovery and continuation after large Day 0 moves
# Positive % = the original move reversed
# Negative % = the original move continued

is_big_drop = (
    events["AR_day0"] <= -SHOCK_SIZE
)

is_big_jump = (
    events["AR_day0"] >= SHOCK_SIZE
)

events["shock_type"] = None

events.loc[
    is_big_drop,
    "shock_type"
] = "Big drop"

events.loc[
    is_big_jump,
    "shock_type"
] = "Big jump"


# Percentage of the original Day 0 move that reversed
events["reversed_pct_day5"] = np.nan
events["reversed_pct_day10"] = np.nan

shock = events["shock_type"].notna()

events.loc[
    shock,
    "reversed_pct_day5"
] = (
    1
    - events.loc[shock, "CAR_0_5"]
    / events.loc[shock, "AR_day0"]
) * 100

events.loc[
    shock,
    "reversed_pct_day10"
] = (
    1
    - events.loc[shock, "CAR_0_10"]
    / events.loc[shock, "AR_day0"]
) * 100


# Recovery / continuation summary
recovery_table = (
    events[shock]
    .groupby("shock_type")
    .agg(
        events=("event_id", "count"),

        median_reversed_pct_day5=(
            "reversed_pct_day5",
            "median"
        ),

        median_reversed_pct_day10=(
            "reversed_pct_day10",
            "median"
        )
    )
)

recovery_table[
    "fully_reversed_by_day10_pct"
] = (
    events[shock]
    .groupby("shock_type")[
        "reversed_pct_day10"
    ]
    .apply(
        lambda s: (s >= 100).mean() * 100
    )
)

display(
    recovery_table.round(1)
)

Benchmarking Against Random Trading Days¶

Persistence can be misleading.

Even on ordinary trading days, stock prices move up and down and some moves will naturally continue for several days.

To provide a simple benchmark, I randomly select 20 trading-day windows for each event's stock and calculate the same persistence measure.

I also compare news events with random days having similar first-move sizes.

This gives a more useful context than looking at event persistence alone.

In [27]:
random.seed(42)

abnormal_arrays = {
    t: abnormal[t].to_numpy()
    for t in tickers
}

last_start = len(prices) - 11

random_rows = []

for _, event in events.iterrows():

    for _ in range(20):

        start = random.randint(
            1,
            last_start
        )

        window = abnormal_arrays[
            event["ticker"]
        ][
            start:
            start + 11
        ]

        if np.isnan(window).any():
            continue

        random_rows.append({
            "AR_day0": window[0],
            "CAR_0_10": window.sum()
        })


random_days = pd.DataFrame(
    random_rows
)

random_days["ratio_day10"] = (
    random_days["CAR_0_10"]
    /
    random_days["AR_day0"]
)

random_days["persisted"] = (
    random_days["ratio_day10"]
    >= PERSIST_RATIO
).astype(float)


bands = [
    0,
    0.01,
    0.02,
    1
]

band_names = [
    "under 1%",
    "1% to 2%",
    "over 2%"
]

events["move_size"] = pd.cut(
    events["AR_day0"].abs(),
    bands,
    labels=band_names,
    right=False
)

random_days["move_size"] = pd.cut(
    random_days["AR_day0"].abs(),
    bands,
    labels=band_names,
    right=False
)


check_table = pd.DataFrame({

    "news events: % persisted":
        events.groupby(
            "move_size",
            observed=True
        )["persisted"].mean() * 100,

    "random days: % persisted":
        random_days.groupby(
            "move_size",
            observed=True
        )["persisted"].mean() * 100,

    "number of events":
        events.groupby(
            "move_size",
            observed=True
        )["event_id"].count()
})

check_table[
    "difference (points)"
] = (
    check_table.iloc[:, 0]
    -
    check_table.iloc[:, 1]
)

check_table.round(1)

Statistical Analysis¶

After exploring the patterns visually, I use statistical tests to check whether the average reaction is different from zero.

A one-sample t-test compares the average abnormal return with zero.

I report:

  • sample size,
  • average reaction,
  • t-statistic,
  • p-value,
  • Bonferroni-adjusted p-value.

Because multiple tests are performed, the Bonferroni adjustment provides a more conservative interpretation.

I also repeat the analysis after keeping only one event per company per trading day because several events may share the same stock return.

In [28]:
def run_tests(data):

    rows = []

    for name, col in summary_columns.items():

        values = data[col].dropna()

        t_stat, p_value = (
            stats.ttest_1samp(
                values,
                0
            )
        )

        rows.append({
            "measure": name,
            "events": len(values),
            "average %":
                values.mean() * 100,
            "t-statistic": t_stat,
            "p-value": p_value
        })

    result = pd.DataFrame(rows)

    result[
        "p-value (Bonferroni)"
    ] = (
        result["p-value"]
        * len(result)
    ).clip(upper=1)

    result[
        "significant at 5%?"
    ] = np.where(
        result[
            "p-value (Bonferroni)"
        ] < 0.05,
        "Yes",
        "No"
    )

    return result


tests_all = run_tests(
    events
)

one_per_day = events.drop_duplicates(
    [
        "ticker",
        "reaction_date"
    ]
)

tests_one_per_day = run_tests(
    one_per_day
)

    "ALL EVENTS (",
    len(events),
    ")"
)

)

print(
    "ONE EVENT PER COMPANY PER DAY (",
    len(one_per_day),
    ")"
)

display(
    tests_one_per_day.round(4)
)

# Pre-event check:
# Did the stock already move before the identified news day?

before = events[
    "AR_before"
].dropna()

t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_1samp(
    before,
    0
)

average_before = (
    before.mean() * 100
)

print(
    f"Average abnormal return on Day -1: "
    f"{average_before:+.3f}% "
    f"(p-value = {p_value:.3f})"
)

if p_value < 0.05:
    print(
        "Finding: Day -1 is statistically different from zero."
    )

    print(
        "Interpretation: part of the observed reaction "
        "may have occurred before the headline was detected."
    )
else:
    print(
        "Finding: Day -1 is not statistically different from zero."
    )

EDA by Event Category¶

The next stage of the EDA asks:

Do different types of business news produce different stock-market reactions?

I compare:

  • Day 0 abnormal return,
  • Day 10 abnormal return,
  • CAR 0-10,
  • percentage of positive Day 0 reactions,
  • persistence,
  • reversal behaviour.

This helps move the analysis from an overall market reaction to business-event-level insights.

In [30]:
events["positive_day0"] = (
    events["AR_day0"] > 0
).astype(float)

events.loc[
    events["AR_day0"].isna(),
    "positive_day0"
] = np.nan


def summarise(group_column):

    table = (
        events
        .groupby(group_column)
        .agg(
            events=("event_id", "count"),

            avg_day0_pct=(
                "AR_day0",
                "mean"
            ),

            avg_day10_pct=(
                "AR_day10",
                "mean"
            ),

            avg_CAR_0_10_pct=(
                "CAR_0_10",
                "mean"
            ),

            positive_day0_pct=(
                "positive_day0",
                "mean"
            ),

            persisted_pct=(
                "persisted",
                "mean"
            ),

            median_reversed_pct_day10=(
                "reversed_pct_day10",
                "median"
            ),
        )
    )

    for col in [
        "avg_day0_pct",
        "avg_day10_pct",
        "avg_CAR_0_10_pct",
        "positive_day0_pct",
        "persisted_pct"
    ]:

        table[col] = (
            table[col] * 100
        )

    return table.sort_values(
        "events",
        ascending=False
    )


category_summary = summarise(
    "event_category"
)

category_summary.round(2)

EDA by Company¶

I also compare the reaction patterns across the 20 companies.

The purpose is not to rank companies as investments.

Instead, I want to understand whether the same type of news appears to produce different reaction patterns across companies.

The comparison includes:

  • average Day 0 abnormal return,
  • average CAR 0-10,
  • percentage of reactions that persisted,
  • and the number of events available for each company.

Event counts are shown alongside the results because a company with very few events should not be interpreted in the same way as one with a much larger sample.

Key Findings¶

The following section generates the final findings directly from the analysis results.

This avoids manually typing numbers into the conclusion and ensures that the written findings remain connected to the actual dataset.

Questions answered¶

  1. How large was the average Day 0 reaction?
  2. Did the reaction remain significant over the following days?
  3. How many reactions persisted until Day 10?
  4. How much did large drops recover?
  5. How much did large jumps give back?
  6. Which event category had the highest and lowest average CAR?
  7. How did news-event persistence compare with random trading days?

The results should be interpreted as observational associations, not proof that the news event alone caused the stock movement.

SAMPLE: 1109 events, 20 companies, news from 2025.

DAY 0: on average the stock moved +0.16% versus the market (significant: No).
CAR 0-10: average +1.01% (Bonferroni-significant: Yes).
PERSISTENCE: 54.5% of reactions were still at least half-size on Day 10.
PRE-EVENT TIMING: Day -1 abnormal return was +0.289% (p = 0.004).
This suggests that part of the observed reaction may have occurred before the headline was detected.

RECOVERY: after big drops (n=274), the median reversal by Day 10 was 48%.
CONTINUATION: after big jumps (n=311), the median reversal measure was -8%.
A negative value means the original jump continued rather than reversing.

CATEGORIES: highest 10-day CAR = Legal / Regulatory (+2.38%), lowest = Leadership (-0.32%).

PLAIN-ENGLISH CONCLUSION:
The average immediate reaction was relatively small, while the cumulative abnormal return over 10 trading days was positive. However, the significant Day -1 movement shows that some of the observed reaction may have occurred before the headline was detected. The results should therefore be interpreted as observational associations rather than proof that the news itself caused the stock movement.

Limitations and Interpretation¶

This project is designed as a practical data-analysis study, so the results should be interpreted carefully.

1. News timestamp limitation¶

GDELT records when it first observed an article. This may not be the exact time when the underlying news was released.

2. Closing-price limitation¶

Day 0 is based on daily closing prices. If news was published during trading hours, part of the Day 0 movement may have happened before the headline was observed.

3. Market benchmark¶

SPY is used as a simple market benchmark. A more advanced financial model could adjust for each company's beta and other risk factors.

4. Event independence¶

Several events can occur for the same company on the same trading day. Therefore, the analysis also includes tests using one event per company per day.

5. Keyword-based categorisation¶

Event categories are created using keyword rules rather than manually reading every article. Some headlines may therefore be categorised incorrectly.

6. Limited sample¶

The analysis covers 20 large companies and one year of news. Results may not generalise to other companies, sectors or time periods.

Final Project Summary¶

This project demonstrates a complete data-analyst workflow:

Extract → financial news and stock-price data

Transform → clean, map, filter, categorise and deduplicate

EDA → explore event distributions, stock reactions, categories and companies

Analyse → abnormal returns, CAR, persistence and recovery

Statistical Analysis → t-tests, Bonferroni adjustment and random-day comparison

Visualise → reaction curves, category comparisons and company comparisons

Load / Report → Power BI-ready analytical CSV files

Main skills demonstrated¶

Python • Pandas • NumPy • Data Cleaning • Data Transformation • ETL-style Data Preparation • Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) • Statistical Analysis • Financial Data Analysis • Data Visualization • Power BI

Load Analytical Outputs for Power BI¶

The final stage of the data workflow is to prepare clean analytical outputs for reporting.

The analysis tables are exported as CSV files so they can be loaded directly into Power BI.

from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import FileLink, display

print("SEARCHING FOR POWER BI CSV FILES...")
print("=" * 60)

file_names = [
    "events_with_reactions.csv",
    "event_window_long.csv",
    "category_summary.csv",
    "company_summary.csv",
    "tests_all_events.csv",
    "tests_one_event_per_day.csv",
    "random_day_check.csv",
    "recovery_summary.csv",
    "cleaning_steps.csv"
]

# Search common locations
search_locations = [
    Path.cwd(),
    Path.home() / "outputs",
    Path.home() / "Desktop",
    Path.home() / "Desktop" / "Stock_Market_Reaction_PowerBI",
]

found_files = {}

for folder in search_locations:
    if folder.exists():
        for name in file_names:
            matches = list(folder.rglob(name))
            for match in matches:
                found_files[name] = match
                break

print()

for name in file_names:
    if name in found_files:
        path = found_files[name]
        print(f"✓ {name}")
        print(f"  Location: {path.resolve()}")
        display(FileLink(str(path)))
    else:
        print(f"✗ {name} - NOT FOUND")

print()
print("Files found:", len(found_files), "of", len(file_names))

# CREATE CLICKABLE POWER BI DOWNLOAD LINKS
# ============================================================

from pathlib import Path
import shutil
from IPython.display import FileLink, display

# Where the CSV files are currently saved
SOURCE_FOLDER = Path(r"C:\Users\User\outputs")

# Create a Power BI folder beside the notebook
DOWNLOAD_FOLDER = Path("PowerBI_Outputs")
DOWNLOAD_FOLDER.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

files = [
    "events_with_reactions.csv",
    "event_window_long.csv",
    "category_summary.csv",
    "company_summary.csv",
    "tests_all_events.csv",
    "tests_one_event_per_day.csv",
    "random_day_check.csv",
    "recovery_summary.csv",
    "cleaning_steps.csv"
]

print("POWER BI DOWNLOAD FILES")
print("=" * 60)

for filename in files:

    source = SOURCE_FOLDER / filename
    destination = DOWNLOAD_FOLDER / filename

    if source.exists():

        # Copy the CSV beside the notebook
        shutil.copy2(source, destination)

        print(f"✓ {filename}")

        # Create clickable Jupyter link
        display(
            FileLink(
                str(destination)
            )
        )

    else:
        print(f"✗ {filename} - NOT FOUND")

# ============================================================
# CONVERT EXISTING CSV OUTPUTS TO REAL EXCEL FILES
# ============================================================

from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import FileLink, display
import pandas as pd

# Existing CSV files
SOURCE_FOLDER = Path(r"C:\Users\User\outputs")

# Final Excel files will be placed beside the notebook
POWERBI_FOLDER = Path("PowerBI_Final")
POWERBI_FOLDER.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

files = [
    "events_with_reactions.csv",
    "event_window_long.csv",
    "category_summary.csv",
    "company_summary.csv",
    "tests_all_events.csv",
    "tests_one_event_per_day.csv",
    "random_day_check.csv",
    "recovery_summary.csv",
    "cleaning_steps.csv"
]

print("CREATING POWER BI EXCEL FILES")
print("=" * 60)

for csv_name in files:

    csv_path = SOURCE_FOLDER / csv_name

    if not csv_path.exists():
        print(f"X {csv_name} - NOT FOUND")
        continue

    # Read the existing CSV
    df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)

    # Change .csv to .xlsx
    xlsx_name = csv_name.replace(".csv", ".xlsx")
    xlsx_path = POWERBI_FOLDER / xlsx_name

    # Create a genuine Excel workbook
    df.to_excel(
        xlsx_path,
        sheet_name="Data",
        index=False,
        engine="openpyxl"
    )

    print(f"✓ {xlsx_name}  {df.shape}")

    # Clickable Jupyter download link
    display(FileLink(str(xlsx_path)))

print()
print("DONE")
print("Excel folder:", POWERBI_FOLDER.resolve())
